name: CTET Paper 1
fullName: Central Teacher Eligibility Test – Paper I (Primary Stage, Classes I–V)
frequency: Usually twice a year (sessions are sometimes skipped or shifted)
approxCandidates: ≈10.65 lakh appeared for Paper 1 in the Feb 2026 session (Papers 1 + 2 together: 26.5 lakh registered, 23.2 lakh appeared)
eligibility: Senior Secondary (50%) plus a 2-year D.El.Ed or 4-year B.El.Ed (final-year students may apply), or an equivalent qualification under NCTE norms. No upper age limit, and the certificate is valid for life.

pattern.notes: Real paper: 150 MCQs of 1 mark each, no negative marking, 2½ hours. Qualifying marks are 60% (90/150) for General and 55% (82/150) for SC/ST/OBC/PwD. Candidates choose Language I and Language II from 20 languages, and they must be different. This mock uses English as Language I and Hindi as Language II. The question bank holds 60 original questions (12 per section), so a mock built from it is a scaled-down version of the full 150-question paper. About half of each Maths, EVS and Language section is pedagogy.

trendAnalysis.summary: This analysis covers the Jul 2024, Dec 2024 and Feb 2026 sessions. No CTET exam was held in calendar 2025: the Dec-2025 cycle was conducted on 8 Feb 2026. Overall difficulty is easy to moderate. CDP and the pedagogy halves of Maths and EVS decide the score, and they increasingly use classroom-scenario and NCF-2005/NEP-2020 based questions rather than definitions. Inclusive education (RPwD Act, learning disabilities), assessment for learning, and Piaget/Vygotsky applications are high-yield in CDP. Maths content stays at primary level (place value, fractions, time, measurement, patterns, data), while pedagogy focuses on error analysis and Van Hiele levels. EVS content is drawn from NCERT Looking Around (Classes III–V) themes such as animals, water, shelter and travel. The Feb 2026 Paper 1 pass rate was 33.69%.

questions.question: A four-year-old insists that the moon follows her when she walks because it wants to play with her. According to Piaget, this belief is an example of:
questions.explanation: In Piaget's pre-operational stage (2–7 years), children believe that lifeless objects have life, feelings and intentions. This is called animism.

relevance.note: Classic CTET 'moon follows me' animism scenario; distractors are other Piagetian terms

questions.question: A child says, "I will not take my friend's eraser without asking because the teacher will punish me." According to Kohlberg, the child's reasoning reflects the:
questions.explanation: The child judges the action by its consequence (punishment). This is Stage 1 of Kohlberg's pre-conventional level.

relevance.note: Faithful Kohlberg statement-to-stage item as set in CTET; fear of punishment cue is standard

questions.question: A baby gains control over the head and neck before gaining control over the legs. This illustrates the:
questions.explanation: Development proceeds from head to tail (cephalocaudal). The proximodistal principle describes development from the centre of the body outward.

relevance.note: Head-before-legs cephalocaudal is a staple CTET development-principle item; proximodistal is the right trap

questions.question: According to Howard Gardner, a child who easily understands the feelings of classmates and works well in groups shows strength in which intelligence?
questions.explanation: Interpersonal intelligence is the ability to understand and interact effectively with others. Intrapersonal intelligence concerns understanding oneself.

relevance.note: Gardner profile-to-intelligence as in CTET; intrapersonal is the expected trap

questions.question: A teacher always asks girls to sweep the classroom and boys to carry the benches. This practice reflects:
questions.explanation: Assigning tasks according to fixed notions of what boys and girls should do reinforces gender stereotypes.

relevance.note: Chore allocation by gender -> stereotyping is a recurring CTET scenario

questions.question: The main purpose of 'assessment for learning' is to:
options: Give ongoing feedback that helps improve teaching and learning
Compare the performance of different schools
Certify students for promotion to the next class
Rank students at the end of the year
questions.explanation: Assessment for learning (formative assessment) happens during instruction and uses feedback to improve learning. Ranking and certification are summative purposes.

relevance.note: Assessment for learning purpose is asked almost every CTET cycle; distractors are summative uses

questions.topic: Inclusive Education & Children with Special Needs
questions.question: A child of average intelligence has persistent difficulty in decoding words, reverses letters while reading and reads very slowly. The child most likely has:
questions.explanation: Dyslexia is a specific learning disability that affects reading and word decoding. Dyscalculia affects number skills, dysgraphia affects writing, and dyspraxia affects motor coordination.

relevance.note: Letter reversal/decoding -> dyslexia, exact CTET symptom-to-disorder pattern

questions.question: From a constructivist point of view, the errors children make while learning are best seen as:
options: Unimportant details that the teacher should ignore
Signs of carelessness that must be penalised
Windows into children's thinking that help the teacher plan instruction
questions.explanation: Errors reveal children's reasoning and misconceptions, so teachers use them diagnostically.

relevance.note: 'Errors as windows into thinking' is one of the most repeated CTET CDP ideas

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"Every monsoon, the village of Kalpur faced the same problem: the only road to the school turned into a stream of mud, and children often missed classes for weeks. In 2019, a group of parents decided they would not wait any longer. Using stones from a nearby quarry and labour donated on weekends, they built a raised footpath along the edge of the fields. The work took four months. Today, attendance during the rainy season is almost as high as in any other season, and the footpath is maintained by the students themselves, who take turns clearing it every Saturday."

Why did children often miss classes in Kalpur?
options: The quarry blocked the road to the school
The road to school turned into mud during the monsoon
Parents needed them to work in the fields
The school was closed during the rainy season
questions.explanation: The passage says the only road to school 'turned into a stream of mud' every monsoon, so children missed classes.

relevance.note: Factual detail from short prose passage; matches CTET Language I comprehension

questions.question:
Read the stanza and answer.

"The old banyan by the river stands,
It holds the evening in its hands;
The birds come home, the shadows creep,
And all the village falls asleep."

The line 'It holds the evening in its hands' contains which poetic device?
questions.explanation: The banyan tree is given a human action (holding something in its hands). This is personification.

relevance.note: Personification in a poem line matches CTET poem-based items

questions.question:
Read the stanza and answer.

"The old banyan by the river stands,
It holds the evening in its hands;
The birds come home, the shadows creep,
And all the village falls asleep."

The rhyme scheme of the stanza is:
questions.explanation: stands/hands rhyme (a, a) and creep/asleep rhyme (b, b), so the scheme is aabb.

relevance.note: Rhyme scheme stands/hands, creep/asleep = aabb; CTET poem item

questions.question: According to Stephen Krashen, children acquire a language most effectively when they:
options: Are corrected immediately for every error
Receive plenty of comprehensible input in a low-anxiety environment
Translate every sentence into their mother tongue
Memorise grammar rules before using the language
questions.explanation: Krashen's Input Hypothesis and Affective Filter Hypothesis say that acquisition happens through comprehensible input when anxiety is low.

relevance.note: Krashen comprehensible input/affective filter is a regular CTET pedagogy item

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate way to assess the speaking skills of Class 4 learners?
options: A role-play or show-and-tell assessed with a simple rubric
questions.explanation: Speaking is assessed through actual oral performance. Role-play or show-and-tell, judged against criteria such as fluency and clarity, does this.

relevance.note: Role play with rubric for speaking assessment, CTET-style assessment item

questions.question: The 'whole language' approach to teaching English in the primary classes emphasises:
options: Learning language through meaningful, authentic texts and contexts
Drilling isolated letters and sounds before any reading
Translating texts word by word into the mother tongue
Memorising lists of words and their spellings
questions.explanation: The whole language approach treats language as a whole system of meaning and uses real stories, conversations and texts instead of fragmented drills.

relevance.note: Whole-language approach definition as asked in CTET English pedagogy

questions.question: Which activity best develops the listening skill of Class 3 learners?
options: Writing the spellings of difficult words
Listening to a story and then arranging picture cards in the order of events
questions.explanation: Sequencing pictures after listening requires children to attend to and understand spoken input, so it builds listening comprehension.

relevance.note: Listening activity choice with plausible distractors; CTET-like

questions.question:
गद्यांश पढ़कर प्रश्न का उत्तर दीजिए।

"पानी हमारे जीवन का आधार है। धरती पर उपलब्ध कुल जल का बहुत छोटा भाग ही पीने योग्य है। बढ़ती जनसंख्या और लापरवाही के कारण यह सीमित भंडार तेज़ी से घट रहा है। यदि हम वर्षा के जल का संचयन करें, नलों को खुला न छोड़ें और नदियों को प्रदूषित होने से बचाएँ, तो आने वाली पीढ़ियों के लिए भी पर्याप्त जल बचा रहेगा।"

गद्यांश के अनुसार पीने योग्य जल का भंडार घटने का मुख्य कारण क्या है?
questions.explanation: गद्यांश में स्पष्ट लिखा है कि 'बढ़ती जनसंख्या और लापरवाही के कारण' सीमित भंडार घट रहा है।

relevance.note: गद्यांश से कारण पूछना — CTET हिंदी भाषा-I का मानक प्रश्न

relevance.note: बाल-साहित्य से पठन-रुचि — CTET pedagogy item, distractors somewhat weak

questions.question: कक्षा 3 के बच्चों की मौखिक अभिव्यक्ति का आकलन करने का सबसे उपयुक्त तरीका है —

relevance.note: मौखिक अभिव्यक्ति आकलन via बातचीत — CTET assessment item

questions.question: What is the difference between the place value and the face value of 7 in the number 47,215?
questions.explanation: Place value of 7 = 7000 and face value = 7. Difference = 7000 − 7 = 6993.

relevance.note: Place value minus face value 7000-7=6993 with 0/7007 traps; CTET maths classic

questions.question: Which of the following fractions is the greatest: 3/4, 5/8, 2/3, 7/12?

relevance.note: Fraction comparison; in-syllabus but plain computation rather than CTET's misconception framing

questions.question: A train leaves a station at 10:45 a.m. and reaches its destination at 2:20 p.m. on the same day. How long is the journey?
questions.explanation: 10:45 a.m. → 1:45 p.m. is 3 h, and 1:45 p.m. → 2:20 p.m. is 35 min. Total = 3 h 35 min.

relevance.note: a.m.-p.m. elapsed time 3h35m with 4h35 trap; CTET maths type

questions.question: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 8 m wide. How much wire is needed to fence it with 3 rounds of wire?
questions.explanation: Perimeter = 2(12 + 8) = 40 m. For 3 rounds, 3 × 40 = 120 m.

relevance.note: Fencing with rounds, area 96 as trap; faithful CTET mensuration

questions.question: What comes next in the pattern 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, …?
questions.explanation: The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, so the next difference is 11 and 26 + 11 = 37. (Equivalently, the terms are n² + 1.)

relevance.note: Odd-difference series 2,5,10,17,26 -> 37; CTET pattern item

questions.question: Add: 3 kg 250 g + 1 kg 875 g = ?
questions.explanation: 250 g + 875 g = 1125 g = 1 kg 125 g. Then 3 kg + 1 kg + 1 kg = 5 kg. Total = 5 kg 125 g.

relevance.note: kg-g addition with carry 5 kg 125 g; distractors from carry errors as in CTET

questions.question: In a pictograph, one symbol stands for 4 students. Class A is shown by 6½ symbols and Class B by 4 symbols. How many more students are in Class A than in Class B?
questions.explanation: Class A = 6.5 × 4 = 26 and Class B = 4 × 4 = 16. Difference = 10.

relevance.note: Pictograph with half symbol and scale 4 -> 10; faithful CTET data-handling item

questions.topic: Place of Maths in Curriculum & Language of Maths
questions.question: According to NCF 2005, the main goal of mathematics education in school is:
options: Mathematisation of the child's thought processes
questions.explanation: NCF 2005 states that the main goal is the mathematisation of the child's thinking, that is, developing the ability to think and reason mathematically.

relevance.note: NCF 2005 'mathematisation' goal is asked repeatedly in CTET maths pedagogy

questions.question: A child writes 46 − 28 = 22. What is the most likely reason for the error?
options: The child has not memorised multiplication tables
The child copied the numbers incorrectly
In each column the child subtracts the smaller digit from the larger one instead of regrouping
The child added the numbers instead of subtracting them
questions.explanation: The child computed 8 − 6 = 2 in the ones column and 4 − 2 = 2 in the tens column. This is the classic 'smaller-from-larger' error: the child did not regroup. The correct answer is 18. Adding would give 74.

relevance.note: Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug 46-28=22; exactly CTET error-analysis format

questions.question: Which task best assesses a Class 4 child's conceptual understanding of fractions?
options: Shade 3/4 of a figure in two different ways and explain why both are correct
Recite that a fraction is 'numerator over denominator'
Write the definition of a fraction
Copy the fractions written on the blackboard
questions.explanation: Representing a fraction in more than one way and justifying it shows understanding, not just recall.

relevance.note: Conceptual-understanding task choice; correct option stands out but CTET-faithful

questions.question: A child identifies a figure as a 'square' because 'it looks like a window', but cannot describe any of its properties. According to the van Hiele model, the child is at the level of:
questions.explanation: At van Hiele Level 0 (visualisation), shapes are recognised by their overall appearance and not by their properties. Properties are noticed at Level 1 (analysis).

relevance.note: van Hiele visualisation from 'looks like a window' reasoning; CTET favourite

questions.topic: Family & Friends (relationships, animals, plants, work & play)
questions.question: Which bird stitches the edges of leaves together with plant fibre to make its nest?
questions.explanation: The tailorbird punctures leaf edges and stitches them together to form a cup-shaped nest. The weaver bird weaves grass strips, the crow piles up twigs, and the koel lays its eggs in a crow's nest.

relevance.note: Tailorbird stitching from NCERT EVS; weaver bird is the right trap

questions.question: 'Tanka' (or 'kund'), an underground tank used to collect rainwater for drinking, is a traditional water-harvesting structure mainly found in:
questions.explanation: Tankas and kunds are typical of arid Rajasthan. Meghalaya is known for bamboo drip irrigation and Himachal Pradesh for kuhls.

relevance.note: Tanka-Rajasthan water-harvesting from NCERT EVS 'Water O Water'; CTET-type

questions.question: When we eat a potato, which part of the plant are we eating?
questions.explanation: A potato is a tuber, which is a swollen underground stem. Its 'eyes' are buds, and buds grow only on stems. A carrot, by contrast, is a root.

relevance.note: Potato is a stem with root trap; CTET EVS plant-part question

questions.question: Houses built on bamboo or wooden stilts, raised above the ground, are most suitable for areas that:

Remain snow-covered for most of the year
questions.explanation: Stilt houses, as in Assam, keep living spaces above flood water and damp ground.

relevance.note: Stilt houses for flood/rain areas from NCERT EVS shelter theme

questions.question: In the morning you stand facing the rising sun. Which direction is behind you?
questions.explanation: The sun rises in the east, so if you face east your back is towards the west.

relevance.note: Sun-direction item from NCERT EVS maps chapter; simple but CTET-type

questions.question: As recommended by NCF 2005, EVS in Classes III to V integrates concepts from:

relevance.note: Letter symmetry (N none); recurring CTET symmetry item

questions.question: A shop opens at 9:30 a.m. and closes at 7:15 p.m. It closes for 45 minutes at lunch time. For how long is the shop open for business in a day?
questions.explanation: From 9:30 a.m. to 7:15 p.m. is 9 hours 45 minutes. Subtracting the 45-minute lunch break gives 9 hours.

relevance.note: Elapsed time minus lunch break = 9 h; two-step time item with 9h45 trap

questions.question: What comes next in the pattern 3, 6, 11, 18, 27, …?
questions.explanation: The differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, so the next difference is 11. 27 + 11 = 38.

relevance.note: Same odd-difference series as item 041 with new numbers; repetitive but valid

questions.question: A child can state that a rectangle has four right angles and opposite sides equal, but cannot yet see that every square is also a rectangle. According to the van Hiele model, the child is at the level of:
questions.explanation: At the analysis level children describe shapes by their properties but do not yet relate classes of shapes. Seeing that a square is a special rectangle needs informal deduction (level 2).

relevance.note: Properties known but no class inclusion -> analysis; precise van Hiele item

questions.question: Which task is most suitable for assessing a Class III child's understanding of addition, rather than mere recall?
options: Make up a story problem that can be solved by 25 + 17
Add 25 and 17 using the column method
questions.explanation: Creating a word problem requires the child to connect the operation with a real situation, which reveals conceptual understanding. The other tasks test procedure or recall.

relevance.note: Make up a story problem for 25+17 assesses understanding; CTET assessment item

questions.question: A child writes 3/4 + 1/2 = 4/6. The error shows that the child:
options: Does not know basic addition facts
Adds numerators and denominators separately, treating fractions like whole numbers
Cannot find the LCM of 2 and 4
questions.explanation: 3 + 1 = 4 and 4 + 2 = 6: the child applies whole-number addition to the numerator and denominator separately, showing no understanding of a fraction as a single quantity. The addition facts themselves are correct.

relevance.note: 3/4+1/2=4/6 adding numerators/denominators; classic CTET misconception item

questions.question: A Class II child has difficulty with "borrowing" (regrouping) in subtraction such as 42 − 17. The most suitable teaching aid is:
options: Bundles of ten sticks and loose sticks
questions.explanation: Opening a bundle of ten to get ten loose sticks shows concretely why one ten is exchanged for ten ones, which is the idea behind regrouping.

relevance.note: Bundles and loose sticks for regrouping; CTET teaching-aid item

questions.topic: Family & Friends (relationships, animals, plants, work & play)
questions.question: Which bird lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, such as crows, instead of building its own nest?
questions.explanation: The koel does not build a nest; it lays its eggs in a crow's nest and the crow raises the chicks. Weaver birds and tailorbirds are skilled nest-builders.

relevance.note: Koel lays eggs in crow nest — NCERT EVS fact asked in CTET

questions.topic: Family & Friends (relationships, animals, plants, work & play)
questions.question: Seeds of which of the following plants are carried away mainly by the wind?
questions.explanation: Madar seeds have fine silky hairs that let them float on the wind. Coconut is dispersed by water, Xanthium by sticking to animals, and balsam pods burst open.

relevance.note: Madar wind dispersal vs balsam/xanthium/coconut; NCERT seed-dispersal item

questions.question: 'Kuhl', a traditional system of channels that carry water from glacier-fed streams to fields, is found mainly in:
questions.explanation: Kuhls are community-built water channels in the hills of Himachal Pradesh (and Jammu). Tankas and kunds are typical of Rajasthan.

relevance.note: Kuhl in Himachal from NCERT EVS; CTET water-harvesting item

questions.question: Who was the first Indian woman to climb Mount Everest?
questions.explanation: Bachendri Pal reached the summit of Everest in 1984. Santosh Yadav climbed it twice, Arunima Sinha was the first female amputee to do so, and Premlata Agarwal climbed it later.

relevance.note: Bachendri Pal from NCERT Class V 'Up You Go'; CTET-faithful

questions.question: Malaria spreads through the bite of the female:
questions.explanation: The malaria parasite (Plasmodium) is transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. Aedes spreads dengue and chikungunya; Culex spreads filariasis.

relevance.note: Anopheles vs Aedes/Culex trap; NCERT EVS malaria content

questions.question: According to NCF 2005, in Classes I and II, environmental concerns are:
options: Taught as a separate subject with its own textbook
Taught as separate science and social science subjects
Integrated with language and mathematics instead of being taught as a separate subject
Kept out of the curriculum until Class III
questions.explanation: NCF 2005 recommends no separate EVS textbook for Classes I–II; the child's environment is used as the context for language and mathematics. EVS becomes a separate integrated subject from Class III.

relevance.note: NCF: EVS integrated with language/maths in Classes I-II; CTET staple

questions.question: Children sort leaves collected from the school garden into groups by shape and size. Which EVS assessment indicator is the teacher mainly observing?
questions.explanation: Grouping objects on the basis of observable features is the indicator "classification" in NCERT's list of EVS assessment indicators.

relevance.note: Leaf sorting -> classification indicator; exact CTET EVS assessment pattern

questions.question: A young child first gains control over movements of the shoulder and upper arm, then of the wrist, and only later of the fingers needed to hold a pencil firmly. This sequence illustrates which principle of development?
options: Development proceeds from general to specific
questions.explanation: Control develops from the centre of the body (shoulder) outwards to the extremities (fingers) – the proximodistal principle. Cephalocaudal is head-to-toe; general-to-specific refers to whole-body responses becoming specific ones.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about development is NOT correct?
options: Physical, cognitive and social-emotional development proceed independently of one another.
Early experiences have a strong influence, but later experiences can modify their effects.
Development continues throughout life, although its rate varies across stages.
Children of the same age may differ widely in their rate of development.
questions.explanation: Development in the different domains is interrelated – e.g. motor development affects social play and language affects thinking. The other three statements are accepted principles.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about socialisation is correct?
options: Children acquire the norms of society mainly through formal instruction by teachers.
The school is the primary agent of socialisation and the family a secondary one.
Socialisation is complete by the time a child begins formal schooling.
Children learn norms, values and roles through interaction with others and also influence the people around them.
questions.explanation: Socialisation is an interactive, lifelong process in which children are active participants. The family is the primary agent and the school a secondary one; formal instruction is only a small part of it.

questions.question: A four-year-old covers her own eyes during a game of hide-and-seek and says, "You can't see me now!" This behaviour is best explained by which feature of pre-operational thought?
questions.explanation: The child assumes that because she cannot see, others cannot see her either – she cannot take another person's perspective. This is egocentrism.

questions.question: A child who has missed his afternoon nap insists, "It can't be afternoon, because I haven't slept yet." According to Piaget, the child is showing:
questions.explanation: The child links two events that usually occur together and treats one as the cause of the other, reasoning from particular to particular. Piaget called this transductive reasoning, typical of the pre-operational stage.

questions.question: Rani believes that all birds can fly. On seeing an ostrich in a video, she changes her idea to "Most birds fly, but some birds cannot." In Piaget's terms, Rani has:
options: Assimilated the new information into her existing schema
Accommodated her schema to the new information
questions.explanation: Rani modifies her existing schema because the new experience does not fit it. Modifying a schema is accommodation; fitting new information into an unchanged schema would be assimilation.

questions.question: Sahil cannot solve a two-step word problem on his own, but succeeds when a classmate asks him, "What do we need to find first?" The gap between what Sahil can do alone and what he can do with such help is called:
questions.explanation: The range between independent performance and performance with guidance is Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. The classmate's prompt is scaffolding and the classmate is the more knowledgeable other.

questions.question: Asked why he helps his younger brother with homework, a child says, "If I help him, he will let me ride his cycle on Sunday." According to Kohlberg, the child's reasoning is at which stage?
questions.explanation: Right action is judged by what one gets in return ('you scratch my back, I'll scratch yours'). This is Stage 2, instrumental purpose and exchange, at the pre-conventional level.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly compares Piaget and Vygotsky?
options: Piaget gave greater importance to culture and social interaction than Vygotsky did.
Vygotsky proposed four universal, invariant stages of cognitive development.
Both held that language plays no role in the development of thought.
Vygotsky held that learning can lead development, whereas Piaget held that development sets limits on what can be learned.
questions.explanation: For Vygotsky, learning with assistance in the ZPD pulls development forward; for Piaget, the child's stage of development limits learning. The universal stages are Piaget's, and Vygotsky stressed culture and language.

questions.question: Arjun easily finds his way back through the lanes of a market he has visited only once, loves jigsaw puzzles and often draws maps of his neighbourhood. According to Gardner, Arjun shows strength in:
questions.explanation: Finding routes, solving jigsaws and drawing maps all involve forming and manipulating mental images of space – visual-spatial intelligence.

questions.question: While building a tower of blocks, a five-year-old mutters to herself, "This big one goes at the bottom… no, not that one." According to Vygotsky, this speech:
options: shows egocentric thinking that has no useful function
helps the child plan and guide her own actions
is social speech addressed to an imaginary listener
indicates a delay in language development
questions.explanation: Vygotsky called this private speech: language turned inward to regulate one's own thinking and behaviour. The view that such speech is merely egocentric and functionless is Piaget's.

questions.question: At the end of a lesson, a teacher gives a three-question exit slip and uses the responses to decide which children need to work on the idea again in small groups the next day. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The evidence is used by the teacher during the learning process to plan the next teaching step – assessment for learning (formative). Assessment as learning involves learners monitoring their own learning.

questions.topic: Inclusive Education & Children with Special Needs
questions.question: A Class 3 child finds it hard to hop, button his shirt and catch a ball; he often bumps into furniture and his letters are poorly formed. He reads and understands stories well. The child is most likely to have:
questions.explanation: Difficulty with planning and coordinating both gross and fine motor movements points to dyspraxia. Dysgraphia is limited to writing, and reading is not affected here.

questions.topic: Inclusive Education & Children with Special Needs
questions.question: A Class 4 child completes class work quickly and frequently asks questions that go beyond the textbook. Which is the most appropriate way to support her?
options: Give her more sums of the same type to keep her busy
Give her open-ended projects and challenging problems related to the topic
Ask her to wait quietly until the others finish so that the class stays together
Make her the class monitor so that she can help maintain discipline
questions.explanation: Enrichment through open-ended, higher-order tasks extends a gifted child's learning. More of the same work, waiting, or non-academic duties do not meet her learning needs.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Frequent use of prizes and marks for every task may reduce children's interest in learning for its own sake.
Reason (R): When rewards are emphasised, children may come to value an activity for the reward rather than for the activity itself.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Over-use of extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation because children attribute their effort to the reward. R explains A.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"Grandmother Lakshmi has kept a seed box under her bed for as long as anyone in the family can remember. It is an ordinary tin box, dented at one corner, but inside it are small cloth bags, each tied with thread and labelled in her careful handwriting: brinjal, bitter gourd, and a red rice that nobody else in the village grows any more. Every year, after the harvest, she chooses the healthiest plants and keeps aside their seeds. 'Shop seeds are good for one season,' she says, 'but these seeds remember our soil.' Last year, when the rains came late and many farmers lost their crops, her red rice survived on the dry upper field. Neighbours who had laughed at her old-fashioned ways came to ask for a handful of seeds. She gave them freely, asking only one thing in return: that they keep some seeds from the next harvest and pass them on to someone else. Now a small group of families meets at her house each April to exchange seeds and stories. The children are given the job of writing the labels, and slowly they are learning the names of plants that their parents had almost forgotten."

Why did the neighbours come to Lakshmi for seeds?
options: Shop seeds were no longer being sold in the village
They wanted their children to learn the names of plants
Her red rice had survived on the dry upper field when the rains came late
She had offered to exchange seeds for stories
questions.explanation: The passage says that when the rains came late her red rice survived, after which the neighbours 'came to ask for a handful of seeds'.

questions.question:
Read the poem and answer.

"The kite climbs up on a string of thread,
A paper bird with a tail of red;
Like a fish it swims through the sea of sky,
And waves to the swallows passing by.
But when the evening wind lies still,
It sleeps upon my window-sill."

Which line of the poem contains a simile?
options: A paper bird with a tail of red
And waves to the swallows passing by
Like a fish it swims through the sea of sky
questions.explanation: A simile makes a comparison using 'like' or 'as': 'Like a fish it swims'. 'A paper bird' is a metaphor, while waving and sleeping are personification.

questions.question: A Class 3 child says, "Yesterday I goed to the market and buyed a ball." This error shows that the child:
options: has not learnt any rules of English grammar
is translating word for word from her mother tongue
is applying a past-tense rule she has worked out to verbs that do not follow it
needs to be drilled immediately on a list of irregular verbs
questions.explanation: Adding '-ed' to 'go' and 'buy' is over-generalisation of the regular past-tense rule. It shows that the child has internalised a rule – a natural, developmental error.

questions.question: Which task is most appropriate for assessing the listening comprehension of Class 2 children?
options: Children copy a short story from the board
Children listen to a short story and arrange picture cards in the order of events
Children answer written multiple-choice questions about a story read aloud
Children recite a poem they have learnt by heart
questions.explanation: Sequencing picture cards shows whether children understood what they heard without depending on reading or writing skills. Written MCQs mix up reading ability with listening.

questions.topic: Challenges of Teaching in Multilingual Classrooms
questions.question: Many children in a Class 3 English class speak Santhali at home. Before reading a story about a market, the teacher asks them to say, in any language, what they buy at their local haat, and writes some of their words on the board next to the English words. This practice:
options: uses children's home languages as a resource for learning English
should be avoided because it slows down the learning of English
creates confusion by mixing two languages
is an example of the grammar-translation method
questions.explanation: Drawing on children's home languages and experiences to build bridges to English treats multilingualism as a resource, as recommended by NCF. It is not grammar-translation, which centres on rules and sentence translation.

questions.question: A child reads a long storybook for pleasure at her own pace, without stopping to look up every unknown word. This kind of reading is called:
questions.explanation: Reading longer texts for pleasure and general understanding is extensive reading. Intensive reading is close study of a short text for detail.

questions.question:
गद्यांश पढ़कर प्रश्न का उत्तर दीजिए।

"हमारे मोहल्ले के नुक्कड़ पर एक छोटा-सा पुस्तकालय है। उसे किसी सरकारी योजना ने नहीं, बल्कि सेवानिवृत्त अध्यापिका सुधा जी ने अपने घर के बरामदे में शुरू किया था। आरंभ में उनके पास केवल पचास पुरानी किताबें थीं, जिन्हें वे बच्चों को एक सप्ताह के लिए पढ़ने देती थीं। धीरे-धीरे लोग अपने घरों की पढ़ी हुई किताबें भी वहाँ छोड़ने लगे। आज उस बरामदे में दो हज़ार से अधिक पुस्तकें हैं। सुधा जी किसी से शुल्क नहीं लेतीं; उनकी एक ही शर्त है कि किताब लौटाते समय बच्चा उसकी कहानी अपने शब्दों में सुनाए। कई अभिभावक पहले इसे समय की बर्बादी मानते थे, पर जब उन्होंने देखा कि बच्चे अब बेझिझक बोलने लगे हैं और उनके लेखन में भी नए-नए शब्द आने लगे हैं, तो उनकी राय बदल गई।"

सुधा जी के पुस्तकालय की एकमात्र शर्त क्या है?
options: किताब एक सप्ताह के भीतर लौटाई जाए
बच्चे हर महीने एक नई किताब दान करें
किताब लौटाते समय बच्चा उसकी कहानी अपने शब्दों में सुनाए
अभिभावक पुस्तकालय के लिए थोड़ा शुल्क दें
questions.explanation: गद्यांश में लिखा है — "उनकी एक ही शर्त है कि किताब लौटाते समय बच्चा उसकी कहानी अपने शब्दों में सुनाए।" एक सप्ताह की बात आरंभिक व्यवस्था के लिए कही गई है, शर्त के रूप में नहीं।

"गाँव के तालाब के किनारे हर शाम बच्चों का जमघट लगता था। कोई मछलियों को दाना डालता, तो कोई काग़ज़ की नावें तैराता। पिछले कुछ वर्षों में तालाब में प्लास्टिक की थैलियाँ और कचरा जमा होने लगा। पानी से दुर्गंध आने लगी और बच्चों ने वहाँ जाना छोड़ दिया। तब कक्षा पाँच के विद्यार्थियों ने अपने अध्यापक के साथ मिलकर एक योजना बनाई। उन्होंने घर-घर जाकर लोगों से बात की, कपड़े के थैले बनाकर बाँटे और हर रविवार तालाब की सफ़ाई का अभियान चलाया। पंचायत ने भी तालाब के चारों ओर कूड़ेदान रखवा दिए। तीन महीने बाद तालाब का पानी फिर से साफ़ दिखने लगा और शाम की रौनक लौट आई। बच्चों ने सिद्ध कर दिया कि बदलाव लाने के लिए बड़ा होना ज़रूरी नहीं, सच्ची लगन ज़रूरी है।"

गद्यांश का मुख्य संदेश है —
options: प्लास्टिक पर पूर्ण प्रतिबंध ही एकमात्र उपाय है
बदलाव लाने के लिए उम्र नहीं, सच्ची लगन आवश्यक है
तालाबों की सफ़ाई केवल पंचायत का दायित्व है
बच्चों को तालाब के पास खेलने नहीं जाना चाहिए
questions.explanation: अंतिम वाक्य में स्पष्ट है — "बदलाव लाने के लिए बड़ा होना ज़रूरी नहीं, सच्ची लगन ज़रूरी है।"

questions.question:
अभिकथन (A): बच्चे विद्यालय आने से पहले ही अपनी भाषा की व्यवस्था पर काफ़ी अधिकार प्राप्त कर चुके होते हैं।
तर्क (R): भाषा केवल विद्यालय में औपचारिक शिक्षण के माध्यम से ही सीखी जाती है।

सही विकल्प चुनिए।
options: (A) और (R) दोनों सही हैं तथा (R), (A) की सही व्याख्या करता है।
(A) और (R) दोनों सही हैं, परंतु (R), (A) की सही व्याख्या नहीं करता है।
questions.explanation: बच्चे अपने परिवेश में भाषा का अर्जन स्वाभाविक रूप से कर लेते हैं, इसलिए (A) सही है। भाषा केवल औपचारिक शिक्षण से नहीं सीखी जाती, अतः (R) गलत है।

questions.question: बच्चे अपने आसपास सुनी भाषा से स्वयं नियम बनाकर ऐसे वाक्य भी बोलने लगते हैं जो उन्होंने पहले कभी नहीं सुने। यह तथ्य किसके मत का सबसे अधिक समर्थन करता है?
options: स्किनर — भाषा अनुकरण और पुनर्बलन से सीखी जाती है
थॉर्नडाइक — भाषा प्रयास और त्रुटि से सीखी जाती है
पावलव — भाषा अनुबंधन से सीखी जाती है
नोम चॉम्स्की — बच्चों में भाषा सीखने की जन्मजात क्षमता होती है
questions.explanation: पहले कभी न सुने वाक्य बना लेना केवल अनुकरण से संभव नहीं। चॉम्स्की के अनुसार बच्चों में भाषा-अर्जन की जन्मजात क्षमता होती है, जिससे वे नियम खोजकर नए वाक्य रचते हैं।

questions.question: कक्षा 4 में 'संज्ञा' की अवधारणा पढ़ाने का सबसे उपयुक्त तरीका है —
options: पहले परिभाषा और भेद लिखवाना, फिर उदाहरण देकर अभ्यास कराना
संज्ञा के भेदों की तालिका बनवाकर कंठस्थ कराना
बच्चों द्वारा पढ़ी गई कहानी से व्यक्तियों, वस्तुओं और स्थानों के नाम छाँटवाकर उनसे अवधारणा तक पहुँचाना
व्याकरण की पुस्तक के अभ्यास-प्रश्न हल करवाना
questions.explanation: संदर्भ और प्रयोग से उदाहरणों के आधार पर नियम तक पहुँचना आगमन विधि है, जो इस स्तर पर सबसे उपयुक्त है। परिभाषा से आरंभ करना निगमन विधि है।

questions.question: कक्षा 1 के बच्चे किताब पढ़ते समय चित्रों और संदर्भ के सहारे शब्दों का अनुमान लगाते हैं। शिक्षक को चाहिए कि वह —
options: पहले पूरी वर्णमाला सिखाए, फिर किताब पढ़ने दे
अनुमान लगाने को रोककर अक्षर-अक्षर पढ़वाए
अनुमान लगाने को प्रोत्साहित करे, क्योंकि यह अर्थ बनाने की स्वाभाविक प्रक्रिया है
बच्चों को केवल चित्र-रहित पुस्तकें दे ताकि वे अक्षरों पर ध्यान दें
questions.explanation: पढ़ना अर्थ ग्रहण करने की प्रक्रिया है। संदर्भ और चित्रों से अनुमान लगाना कुशल पाठक की रणनीति है, इसलिए इसे प्रोत्साहित करना चाहिए।

questions.question: कक्षा 2 में मौखिक अभिव्यक्ति के विकास के लिए सबसे उपयुक्त गतिविधि है —
options: पाठ के प्रश्नोत्तर मौखिक रूप से याद कराना
कविता को सुर-ताल के साथ कंठस्थ कराना
कठिन शब्दों का बार-बार शुद्ध उच्चारण कराना
चित्र देखकर उसे अपने अनुभवों से जोड़ते हुए बातचीत करना
questions.explanation: अपने अनुभवों से जुड़ी बातचीत में बच्चे अपने शब्दों में विचार व्यक्त करते हैं। कविता कंठस्थ कराना या प्रश्नोत्तर याद कराना केवल दोहराव है, अभिव्यक्ति नहीं।

questions.question: कक्षा 3 के बच्चों के पठन-कौशल का आकलन करने का सबसे उपयुक्त तरीका है —
options: कोई अपरिचित सरल कहानी पढ़वाकर उस पर बातचीत करना
पाठ के अंत में दिए प्रश्नों के उत्तर लिखवाना
पाठ्यपुस्तक का पहले पढ़ाया हुआ पाठ पढ़वाना
questions.explanation: अपरिचित पाठ से पता चलता है कि बच्चा सचमुच पढ़कर अर्थ ग्रहण कर पा रहा है। पढ़ाया हुआ पाठ स्मृति से भी पढ़ा जा सकता है और श्रुतलेख वर्तनी का आकलन करता है।

questions.question: कक्षा 3 के कुछ बच्चे बोलने और लिखने में 'स' और 'श' का भेद नहीं कर पाते। उपचारात्मक शिक्षण के लिए सबसे उपयुक्त उपाय है —
options: अशुद्ध लिखे शब्दों को बीस-बीस बार लिखवाना
'सब–शब', 'सिला–शिला' जैसे शब्द-युग्मों के खेल और उनके अर्थ-भेद पर बातचीत करना
ध्वनियों के उच्चारण-स्थान के नियम कंठस्थ कराना
इसे अनदेखा करना, क्योंकि यह भेद अपने-आप आ जाएगा
questions.explanation: अर्थ बदलने वाले शब्द-युग्मों से बच्चे ध्वनि-भेद को सुनते, बोलते और समझते हैं। रटाने या बार-बार लिखवाने से समझ नहीं बनती।

questions.question: कक्षा की अधिकतर बच्चों की घर की भाषा भोजपुरी है। बारिश पर हिंदी कविता पढ़ाने से पहले शिक्षक बच्चों से बारिश पर अपनी भाषा का कोई गीत सुनाने को कहता है। शिक्षक का यह कदम —
options: अनुवाद विधि द्वारा कविता का अर्थ स्पष्ट करना है
बहुभाषिकता को कक्षा में संसाधन के रूप में उपयोग करना है
बच्चों के मनोरंजन मात्र के लिए है
मानक हिंदी पर बोली के प्रभाव को कम करने का प्रयास है
questions.explanation: बच्चों की घर की भाषा को कक्षा में स्थान देकर उसे नई भाषा सीखने का आधार बनाना बहुभाषिकता को संसाधन मानना है। यहाँ कविता का अनुवाद नहीं किया जा रहा।

questions.question: What is the difference between the place values of the two 5s in the number 5,32,650?
questions.explanation: Place values: 5,00,000 and 50. Difference = 5,00,000 − 50 = 4,99,950. Zero is the difference of the face values.

questions.question: A ribbon 2 m long is cut into pieces of 18 cm each. How many full pieces are obtained, and how much ribbon is left over?
questions.explanation: 2 m = 200 cm. 200 ÷ 18 = 11 remainder 2 (11 × 18 = 198). Reading the calculator decimal 11.11 as 11 cm, or taking 2 m as 2000 cm, gives the wrong options.

questions.question: Which of the following fractions lies between 1/2 and 3/4?
questions.explanation: 1/2 = 4/8 and 3/4 = 6/8, so 5/8 lies between them. 3/8 is less than 1/2; 4/5 = 0.8 and 7/8 = 0.875 are greater than 3/4.

questions.question: A solid has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices. The solid is a:
questions.explanation: A triangular prism has 2 triangular and 3 rectangular faces (5), 9 edges and 6 vertices. A square pyramid has 5 faces but only 8 edges and 5 vertices.

questions.question: A jug holds 1 L 250 mL of juice. How many glasses of 125 mL each can be filled from 3 such jugs?
questions.explanation: 3 × 1250 mL = 3750 mL; 3750 ÷ 125 = 30. One jug alone gives 10; treating 1 L 250 mL as 1.25 and dividing wrongly gives 300.

questions.question: A square garden has the same perimeter as a rectangular garden measuring 18 m by 10 m. What is the area of the square garden?
questions.explanation: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(18 + 10) = 56 m. Side of square = 56 ÷ 4 = 14 m. Area = 14 × 14 = 196 m². 180 m² is the rectangle's area.

questions.question: Matchsticks are used to make a row of triangles joined side by side: 1 triangle needs 3 sticks, 2 triangles need 5 sticks, 3 triangles need 7 sticks, and so on. How many matchsticks are needed for 10 triangles?
questions.explanation: Each new triangle adds 2 sticks: number of sticks = 2n + 1. For n = 10, 2 × 10 + 1 = 21. 30 assumes no sticks are shared.

questions.question: A teacher wants to check whether Class 3 children understand place value rather than just the steps of addition. Which question is most suitable?
options: In 345, what does the digit 4 stand for? Show it using bundles of ten sticks.
questions.explanation: Asking what the digit stands for and representing it concretely shows whether the child understands that 4 means 4 tens (40). The other tasks can be done by following a procedure.

questions.question: A child says that 0.45 is greater than 0.5 "because 45 is greater than 5". The child's error shows that she:
options: does not know the place value of the whole-number part
confuses decimals with fractions having denominator 5
treats the digits after the decimal point as a whole number
questions.explanation: The child compares 45 and 5 as whole numbers, ignoring that 0.5 = 5 tenths = 50 hundredths, which is more than 45 hundredths.

questions.question: A child writes 23 × 4 = 812. What does the error show?
options: The child does not know the multiplication fact 3 × 4
The child added the digits instead of multiplying them
The child writes each partial product side by side without regrouping by place value
The child multiplied from left to right instead of from right to left
questions.explanation: 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 4 = 8 are both correct facts; the child wrote 8 and 12 next to each other without carrying the 1 ten. The difficulty is with place value and regrouping.

questions.question: A Class 3 child believes that 1/4 of a chapati is bigger than 1/2 of the same chapati "because 4 is bigger than 2". The most suitable remedial activity is:
options: Making the child memorise the rule 'the bigger the denominator, the smaller the fraction'
Folding identical paper circles into halves and quarters and comparing the parts
Using an abacus to compare 2 and 4
questions.explanation: Folding equal wholes lets the child see that a whole shared into more parts gives smaller parts – moving from concrete to abstract. Memorising a rule does not build the concept.

questions.topic: Family & Friends (relationships, animals, plants, work & play)
questions.question: According to the NCERT EVS textbook, ants of a colony move in a line one behind the other because they:
options: follow the leader ant by looking at it
are guided by sounds made by the queen ant
follow the smell left on the way by the ants ahead
questions.explanation: Ants leave a smell (chemical trail) on their path, and the ants that follow use their sense of smell to keep to the same route ('Super Senses', Class V).

questions.topic: Family & Friends (relationships, animals, plants, work & play)
questions.question: Which animal, described in the NCERT EVS book, sleeps about 17 hours a day hanging upside down from the branches of trees and comes down only about once a week?
questions.explanation: The sloth spends most of its life hanging upside down from trees and sleeps about 17 hours a day. Bats also hang upside down but are active fliers at night.

questions.topic: Family & Friends (relationships, animals, plants, work & play)
questions.question: New plants can grow from the leaves of which of the following plants?
questions.explanation: Buds on the leaf margins of Bryophyllum grow into new plants. Potato grows from buds (eyes) on its stem tuber, sugarcane from stem cuttings, and mango from seeds.

questions.question: Which pair contains only rabi crops?
questions.explanation: Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in spring – wheat, mustard, gram. Rice, maize and cotton are kharif crops.

questions.question: Mango pickle made at home can be kept for a year or more mainly because:
options: raw mangoes are sour, so germs cannot grow in them
large amounts of salt and oil stop it from getting spoilt
pickle is always stored in a refrigerator
spices are added to give it colour
questions.explanation: Salt and oil (with drying in the sun) prevent the growth of microbes, which preserves the pickle. Sourness alone does not keep raw mangoes from rotting.

questions.question: Houses in Ladakh are made of stone with thick walls and flat roofs. The flat roofs are suitable there because:
options: heavy snow slides off flat roofs easily
flat roofs need more wood, which is easily available
flat roofs help to collect rainwater for drinking
very little rain falls, and the roofs are used to dry and store things
questions.explanation: Ladakh is a cold desert with little rainfall, so water does not collect on flat roofs; people use them to dry vegetables and fruits and to store wood and fodder ('A Shelter so High!', Class V).

questions.question: The Changpa, a nomadic community of Ladakh, live in portable tents made of yak hair. These tents are called:
questions.explanation: The Changpa live in rebos, tents woven from yak hair that can be put up and taken down as they move with their herds. Bhungas are round mud huts of Kutch.

questions.question: An egg sinks in a glass of tap water but floats after a lot of salt is stirred into the water. This is because:
options: salt enters the egg and fills it with air
salt water pushes the egg up more strongly than plain water
stirring makes the water move upwards
questions.explanation: Dissolving salt makes the water denser, so it exerts a greater upward push on the egg, which then floats. The egg's own weight does not change.

questions.question: In the NCERT EVS chapter about an astronaut's experience in space, it is explained that things in the spaceship float around. This happens because:
options: the air inside the spaceship pushes them up
magnets in the spaceship attract them to the roof
the spaceship is very close to the Sun
things do not feel any pull towards the floor of the spaceship
questions.explanation: In orbit, astronauts and objects experience weightlessness – nothing is pulled towards the floor – so things float ('Sunita in Space', Class V).

questions.question: On a map, 1 cm stands for 2 km. Two villages are 6.5 cm apart on the map. What is the actual distance between them?
questions.explanation: Actual distance = 6.5 × 2 km = 13 km. Dividing by the scale (3.25 km) or adding (8.5 km) are common errors.

questions.question: Early in the morning, Reena stands facing the rising Sun. Which direction is on her left?
questions.explanation: The Sun rises in the east. Facing east, north is on the left, south on the right and west behind.

questions.question: According to the NCERT EVS book, the correct way to prepare ORS at home is to mix in one glass of boiled and cooled water:
options: a pinch of salt and a fistful of sugar
one spoon each of salt and sugar
a pinch of sugar and a fistful of salt
questions.explanation: ORS: a pinch of salt and a fistful of sugar in a glass of boiled and cooled water. The reverse mixture would be far too salty.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): EVS textbooks for Classes III–V are organised around themes such as Food, Water and Shelter rather than separate science and social science chapters.
Reason (R): Children experience their environment as a whole and not in separate subject compartments.

Choose the correct option.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: NCERT organised EVS thematically because young children see their surroundings holistically, so integrating science, social science and environmental education suits their thinking. R explains A.

questions.question: While teaching the theme 'Water', a teacher asks Class IV children to list all the ways water is used in their homes in a day and to estimate how many buckets their family uses. The main purpose of this activity is to:
options: relate the concept to children's daily experiences so that they build their own understanding
develop children's skills of accurate measurement
collect marks for the summative assessment
make children realise that their families waste water
questions.explanation: Starting from children's own lived experience and inquiry is a key learning principle in EVS. The activity is not mainly about measurement, grading or blaming families.

questions.question: A teacher plans a visit to a nearby dairy farm for Class III. Which step before the visit will make it most useful for learning?
options: Giving children a list of facts about cows to memorise before the visit
Asking children to frame questions they would like to ask the people working at the farm
Telling children to copy the textbook chapter on animals
Telling children that they will be tested on the visit
questions.explanation: Framing their own questions gives the visit a purpose, builds on children's curiosity and makes them active inquirers rather than passive visitors.

questions.question: Many NCERT EVS chapters contain questions such as 'Have you ever seen someone…? What did you feel?' The main purpose of these questions is to:
options: check whether children remember the facts given in the chapter
provide ready-made items for the summative test
help children relate the content to their own experiences and express their views, with no single right answer
questions.explanation: Open-ended, experience-based questions encourage children to connect content with their lives, think and express themselves; they have no fixed answers.

questions.question: During a discussion on who does which work in their locality, children argue that cleaning work should not be left to any one group of people. Which EVS assessment indicator is the teacher mainly observing?
questions.explanation: Showing sensitivity to fairness and challenging the idea that certain work belongs to certain groups is the indicator 'concern for justice and equality'.

questions.question: After a walk around the school pond, a child asks, "Why do some birds come to our pond only in winter?" Which EVS assessment indicator does this mainly reflect?
questions.explanation: Raising a 'why' question from one's own observation reflects the indicator 'questioning'. The child has observed, but the behaviour assessed here is asking questions.

questions.question: To help Class III children learn about the different kinds of houses in their own area, the most appropriate learning resource is:
options: a well-made chart showing houses from different states
a documentary video on houses around the world
a model house made by the teacher
a walk around the neighbourhood to observe houses and talk with a mason
questions.explanation: The immediate surroundings and local people are the richest EVS resources: children observe real houses and materials and learn from a resource person in their own context.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the CTET papers of August 2023, January 2024, July 2024 and December 2024 (official question booklets/answer keys as reproduced on coaching sites) and memory-based shift analyses of the February 2026 cycle (no CTET was held in calendar 2025). WebSearch was used for the 2024–2026 analyses (PW, Careers360, Adda247, Prepp); full official papers could not be fetched, so the archetype list also draws on the writer's own knowledge of earlier CTET papers. Patterns are described in our own words; no real question is reproduced. Frequencies are per 30-question section.
